summary: Recruitment assessment platform tooling, Full-stack frontend engineering, Scalable, reliable, accessible assessment systems

motivation_letter.name: Goonja Gandhi
paragraphs: Assessment tooling sits at a unique intersection: it must be both technically reliable and deeply considerate of user experience, since the platform directly shapes how candidates and recruiters experience your company. Building such a system requires understanding not just how to move data efficiently, but how interface choices affect the people using them. This combination of technical precision and human-centred design is what attracted me to this role.

Over five years as a frontend engineer, I have learned that performance and accessibility are not additions to a system—they are foundational to how a platform communicates its values. At TCS, I reduced API calls by 40% through RxJS optimization and achieved zero accessibility violations by treating WCAG compliance as a core architectural requirement, not a checkbox. More recently, I shrank a React application's bundle from 941KB to under 300KB through deliberate code-splitting and rendering strategy, raising its Lighthouse score from 73 to 95. These optimizations matter most when the system supports critical decisions—like assessment and recruitment—where every millisecond of load time and every interaction clarity affects the user's experience.

What drew me deeper into frontend architecture was the need to understand what abstractions are actually solving. I built a reactive state management engine from first principles to understand how React's rendering cycle works beneath the framework API. I engineered NewsAlign, an AI fact-verification platform, integrating RAG pipelines with LangChain and FAISS while managing bundle size and performance concurrently. These projects reflect a practice of looking beneath the tools I use—understanding why caching strategies matter, how rendering decisions cascade through a system, and where complexity genuinely adds value versus where it introduces friction.

In a recruitment tooling context, this approach translates directly: designing interfaces that scale across global teams, ensuring the platform remains reliable under assessment volume, and writing code that others can read, modify, and trust. I am drawn to roles where frontend engineering shapes how systems serve their users, and where technical depth enables, rather than complicates, that service. Thank you for considering my application. I look forward to the opportunity to discuss how I can contribute.
motivation_letter.closing: Thank you for considering my application. I look forward to the opportunity to discuss how I can contribute.

summary: Robotic systems data infrastructure, Full-stack engineer role, end-to-end ownership from capture dashboards to training pipelines

motivation_letter.name: Goonja Gandhi
paragraphs: What makes Revel's work distinctive is the coupling of real-time data capture from physical robotic systems with the infrastructure needed to move that data through labelling, training, and deployment pipelines. This is not a typical application problem—it requires engineering across the full stack, from the UI that operators interact with in the field to the data architecture that feeds machine learning systems. The challenge is not just building features; it is designing systems where UI decisions directly affect data quality, and where the pipeline between device and training cluster shapes what the models can learn.

I have spent the last five years as a frontend engineer, but my trajectory has been deliberately shaped by a question that guides much of my work: what problem is an abstraction solving? When I built NewsAlign, a fact-verification system using semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation, I found myself moving beyond the React layer into how data flows through a system—how information is indexed, retrieved, and reasoned over. I learned that the abstraction of 'fetch and display' obscures real decisions about latency, cost, and retrieval quality that have to be made consciously. Similarly, when I optimized that system's bundle from 941KB to under 300KB and lifted its Lighthouse score from 73 to 95, the work was not just frontend tuning; it required understanding how rendering, caching, and data transfer patterns interact across the entire request cycle.

Over five years at companies like TCS and through my recent full-stack work, I have built React and Angular applications at scale, mentored teams on frontend architecture, and reduced API overhead by 40% through state management strategy. But more relevant to Revel's needs is the experience I have developed in systems where the frontend is not decorative—where UI decisions cascade into backend consequences. Building a capture dashboard for robotic vision systems, or live data-overlay tools that depend on synchronized streams from hardware, requires that same thinking. I understand how to structure state so that real-time data updates propagate efficiently, how to design interactions that survive network latency, and how backend constraints should inform frontend design rather than react to it after the fact.

A role that spans from capture dashboards to the data pipeline between device and training infrastructure appeals to me precisely because it requires ownership across layers. I am not looking for a position where frontend and backend are siloed concerns. I am looking for work where an engineer has to think about the entire path—from what a user sees and interacts with, to how that interaction generates data, to how that data is structured for consumption downstream. That is where my learning over the past years has been leading me, and that is the kind of ownership Revel's role seems to demand. Thank you for considering my application. I look forward to the opportunity to discuss how I can contribute.
